longo.sub: the most profitable price in gaming
longo.nar: The most profitable price in gaming is zero. Free-to-play games make more money than the entire film industry — and today we open the machine to see how.

longo.sub: of players pay for almost everything
longo.nar: Here is the number the industry is built on: in a typical free-to-play game, roughly two percent of players generate the vast majority of revenue. The other ninety-eight play for free — and that is by design.

longo.sub: the players who fund the ocean
longo.nar: The industry calls them whales: players who spend hundreds or thousands a month. Below them, dolphins spend a little. Minnows spend nothing — but they matter more than they think.
Because free players are not freeloaders — they are the product. They fill the lobbies, populate the leaderboards, and give the whales an audience. No crowd, no show.

The stack works in layers: the battle pass converts time into a subscription. Limited-time offers manufacture urgency. And gacha mechanics sell chance itself — a lottery ticket dressed as a treasure chest.
Underneath it all runs one engine: fear of missing out. The shop rotates, the season ends, the skin never returns. The scarcity is artificial — the feeling is real.

Follow a ten-pound purchase: the platform takes its cut first, development and servers take theirs, marketing eats a surprising share — and what remains is why every publisher wants a live-service game.

longo.sub: playing free is a rational choice
longo.nar: Knowing the machine changes the game. Playing free is a perfectly rational choice — you are the audience the whales pay for. And if you do spend, spend on fun, never on fear.
Every game is also a business, and the business shapes the game you play — from matchmaking to map design. Learn to see the machine, and you will never look at a shop screen the same way.
So which one are you — whale, dolphin, or happy minnow? Drop it in the comments, and subscribe to the lab: we dissect the money inside your games, every week.

The industry calls big spenders whales. Free players are the audience the whales perform for.
